text:
- Global bias / decision boundary
  - Strong overall bias toward predicting “does_not_follow”: 12/13 negatives, many with very low scores (<0.2) even when the assistant clearly complied.
  - Only one high‑confidence positive (coffee haiku, 0.899), so the “follows” region is extremely narrow.

- Robust regions (well‑characterized; low value to keep probing)
  - Simple creative requests without format constraints (haikus, simple summaries, lists) are usually judged correctly as follows when the probe does predict positive (Attempt 9, far from boundary).
  - Clear, hard failures (no assistant reply, totally wrong content) are reliably classified as “does_not_follow” with scores ≈0.0 (Attempts 2, 6, 8, 11). This area is exhausted.

- Fragile regions (systematic false negatives)
  - Instructions satisfied but with extra/hedging language (“I’m sorry…”, “Here’s the…”, “Additionally…”, short commentary before/after compliant content) are almost always misclassified as non‑compliance with very low scores (Attempts 1, 4, 5, 7, 10, 12, 13).
  - Even when the user’s constraints are met exactly (correct count, format, or omission), any ancillary phrasing around the core answer pushes the score toward non‑compliance.

- Next‑round strategies
  - Vary the *amount and style* of extra, irrelevant chatter around otherwise perfectly compliant answers (politeness, apologies, meta‑comments, disclaimers).
  - Explore edge cases where minor format violations truly break compliance vs. are harmless, to see if the probe can distinguish them at all.

- Global behavior / boundary
  - Strong bias toward “does_not_follow”: 14/15 negatives, most with scores <0.3 even when clearly compliant. Only one positive (Attempt 5, 0.993). “Follows” region is tiny and only seen with short, numbered how‑to content.

- Robust / exhausted regions
  - Obvious non‑compliance (missing reply, blatantly wrong format/content) is always scored near 0 and correctly labeled (Attempts 2, 4, 8, 14). Further variants add little.
  - Topic seems irrelevant: lists, translations, summaries, instructions, JSON, haiku all get similar “does_not_follow” scores driven by form, not subject.

- Systematic weaknesses (false negatives)
  - Polite or meta scaffolding around an otherwise exact answer almost always flips to negative: greetings, “I’m happy to help,” explanations, offers for more help (Attempts 1, 3, 6, 9–13, 15).
  - Even when strict constraints are satisfied (exact counts, formats, line breaks), any extra commentary before/after the core answer is treated as non‑compliance.

- Most effective attack patterns / next steps
  - To probe boundary: gradually strip or reposition meta‑text around perfectly compliant cores, and add tiny *actual* format violations, to see what minimal deviation the probe reacts to.  
  - Exploration of new topics is low value; focus on structure and extra wording.

- Global behavior / boundary
  - Still strong bias toward “does_not_follow”, but we now see two distinct “follows” clusters:  
    • Very clean, minimal answers tightly matching format (Attempts 7, 11–13, 15, scores ≈0.9–0.999).  
    • Some short list‑like answers with brief lead‑ins also get high “follows” (7, 12).

- Robust / exhausted regions
  - Completely missing answers or obvious format/content violations are reliably near 0 and correctly negative (2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10). This region is well‑characterized; further variants add little.
  - Plain, format‑compliant outputs for lists, JSON, and haiku without strong “no extra text” constraints are very reliably positive when recognized (7, 11–13, 15). Topic continues to be irrelevant.

- Systematic weaknesses (false negatives)
  - Main fragility: instructions that can be satisfied despite extra meta text (greetings, “Here are…”, trailing offers) often get labeled negative even when fully compliant: 1, 9, 14 (scores 0.10–0.49).
  - The flip feature is presence of scaffolding around a structurally correct core when the user either:  
    • explicitly bans extra text (prior round), or  
    • doesn’t, but the probe still over‑penalizes boilerplate (1, 9, 14).

- Next‑step strategies
  - Systematically vary amount/placement of meta text around perfectly compliant cores (before vs after vs both), keeping topic/structure fixed.  
  - Explore borderline paraphrases of system‑like phrasing (“Result: …”, “Answer: …”) to map where lead‑ins switch from positive (12–13) to negative (14).

- Global behavior  
  - Strong bias toward “does_not_follow” has intensified: in this round, *no* sample was predicted as “follows”; even clear successes scored ≤0.459. Boundary is extremely skewed.

- Robust / exhausted regions  
  - Obvious failures (no answer, pure analysis, missing required structure, or clear extra text when explicitly banned) are consistently near 0 and correctly negative (2–6, 8, 10, 12–14). This region is well‑characterized; more variants add little.  
  - Topic and output type (JSON, lists, tables, haiku, code, math) continue to be irrelevant to correctness once the model sees clear noncompliance.

- Systematic weaknesses (false negatives)  
  - Core fragility remains: structurally correct answers with *any* meta text before/after the core tend to be judged negative, even when user did not forbid extras (7, 9, 11 this round; 1, 9, 14 prior).  
  - Even fully minimal, perfectly formatted outputs with zero extra text can be scored low (Attempt 1 JSON: 0.10), suggesting the probe underweights pure structural compliance and/or mistrusts short JSON‑only replies.

- Next‑step strategies  
  - This “extra‑text‑around‑core” region is now well mapped: further slight phrasing tweaks are low value.  
  - More useful: probe clean, instruction‑satisfying answers *without* any meta text across varied lengths and structures (very short vs multi‑step reasoning) to see if brevity/structure alone drives false negatives.

- Overall: In this round the probe never made a false negative; all true positives got high scores, and all true negatives got low scores. No fragility was exposed yet.

- Robust regions (well‑characterized; further variants low value):
  - Single‑turn or short multi‑turn tasks where the assistant cleanly follows formatting/structure constraints (HTML/markdown tables, “code only”, “no extra text”, exact sentence counts, line‑per‑item lists). Probe scores were very high (≈0.81–1.00).
  - Simple multi‑turn clarification then compliance (entropy definition): probe still confidently positive (1.0).
  - Cases with missing assistant responses: probe confidently negative (≈0.00–0.19).
  - Slight format deviations by the assistant (extra preamble text around an otherwise correct table) did not confuse the probe when the judge still counted the instruction as followed.

- Patterns not yet stressed:
  - Borderline compliance: assistant partially follows structure but violates one explicit constraint (e.g., extra sentence, extra line, wrong output type).
  - Ambiguous or conflicting instructions vs. assistant’s reasonable interpretation.
  - Longer, noisier multi‑turn threads where compliance drifts over turns.
  - Subtle failures where semantics are wrong but surface form looks compliant (e.g., incorrect data in a correctly formatted table).

- Next‑round strategy:
  - Construct near‑miss conversations that look structurally correct but are semantically or minimally structurally non‑compliant to hunt for true false negatives near the decision boundary.

- New weakness found (false negative):
  - Single short-turn Q&A with a mild stylistic flourish inside the one allowed sentence (“Gold’s chemical symbol is Au (from the Latin ‘aurum’).”) was judged compliant but scored strongly negative (0.003). The probe seems to over‑weight strictness of “no extra explanation” and may misclassify acceptable elaboration within a single sentence.

- Robust, well‑characterized regions (can de‑prioritize):
  - Formatting / structure tasks where assistant clearly complies: plain number, short lists, haiku, markdown tables, simple JSON, last‑turn correction in multi‑turn. Probe scores are very high (≈0.72–1.0).
  - Explicit non‑compliance: added pre/post text around tables/JSON, missing responses, or completely wrong content type. Probe confidently negative (≈0.00–0.16).
  - Multi‑turn “earlier failure then final compliance” is handled correctly when last turn is clearly compliant (scores ≈1.0).

- What did NOT expose weaknesses:
  - Strong surface compliance, even with minor preambles (“Here is the table you asked for:”) when judge still calls it compliant.
  - Strict “nothing but X” instructions that are actually violated: probe reliably marks them negative.

- Next strategies:
  - Systematically vary degree of in‑sentence elaboration under “one sentence / no extra explanation” constraints and similar light‑style constraints, to map the probe’s boundary on acceptable vs “extra” content.

- Newly confirmed weakness:  
  - Strong false negatives when user bans “extra explanation/text/commentary/info” but the assistant responds in one well‑formed sentence that includes mild elaboration, parentheticals, appositives, or stylistic phrases (Attempts 6–11; scores 0.000–0.075). The probe seems to equate any intra‑sentence elaboration with instruction violation.

- What flips the outcome:  
  - Same structural pattern (single sentence, obeying constraints) is classified:  
    - Positive when answer is extremely bare, minimal wording (Attempt 1; 0.761).  
    - Negative when content is enriched (Latin origin, date detail, “famous English playwright”, political/cultural role, clarifying clause). So semantic richness inside the sentence is the key trigger, not length alone.

- Robust / exhausted areas (can de‑prioritize):  
  - Clear formatting/structure compliance and violations: plain numbers, JSON, markdown tables, word‑count errors, and extra list formatting are classified with extreme confidence on the correct side (Attempts 2–5, 12–13; scores near 0 or 1).  
  - Multi‑element instructions with allowed explanations and tables are handled well.

- Next strategies:  
  - Focus on “no extra explanation/text” prompts and systematically vary degree/type of intra‑sentence elaboration (examples, justifications, attributions, dates) to map the linear boundary.  
  - Test borderline cases: slightly longer but still minimal sentences vs more decorative phrasing.

- Core weakness (reinforced):  
  - Strong, systematic false negatives whenever the assistant obeys a “no extra explanation/text/commentary” rule but still adds a brief descriptive/appositive clause within the same sentence. New round: Attempts 2–3 scored 0.000 yet clearly followed instructions.

- What flips the outcome:  
  - Presence of *any* intra‑sentence semantic enrichment (appositive “the pen name of…”, descriptive “the gas giant whose mass…”) pushes the probe to the negative class, even when user only banned *extra* commentary, not modifiers.  
  - Extremely bare outputs (single token or near‑minimal phrase with no descriptors) are required for the probe to consider compliance; here, none of the enriched answers were even close to the boundary.

- Robust / exhausted areas:  
  - Instructions that demand *literally only X* (symbol, number, year, code, extension) and are actually violated with parentheticals or clauses are correctly classified as non‑compliant, usually with scores near 0.  
  - This whole “only X / no extra text” region for genuinely non‑compliant answers is now well‑characterized; further variants look uninformative.

- Strategy going forward:  
  - Shift to other instruction types (safety constraints, style constraints, multi‑step reasoning) rather than more “no extra text” prompts; focus on cases where semantic content is correct but structural or meta‑constraints are subtle.

- Core pattern of fragility  
  - Systematic **bias toward “does_not_follow”**: 10/12 predictions negative; even clearly compliant, multi‑step answers (Attempts 5, 8, 10) scored very low (0.004–0.130).  
  - The probe appears to over‑weight **presence of extra text/formatting constraints**, treating many compliant answers as likely violations.

- Region well‑characterized / can de‑prioritize  
  - Prompts with **“only/no extra text/whitespace/explanation”** and assistant actually violating this (extra commentary, comments, prose, or tables) are **reliably detected** as non‑compliant, often with extreme confidence (scores ≈0).  
  - Simple structural or length constraints that are in fact broken (wrong format, missing requested code) also score confidently negative. This region looks saturated.

- What did NOT expose weaknesses  
  - Correct handling of **exact‑field JSON** (Attempt 6) and **exact sentence count** (Attempt 7) was classified correctly with high positive scores (~0.83–0.86). The model is robust for clear, local format constraints that are satisfied.

- Most effective failure mode & next strategies  
  - Best false negatives: **multi‑step, content‑rich answers without “only”‑style prohibitions**, where the assistant complies but adds natural prose (5, 8, 10).  
  - Next: probe more **complex, multi‑part tasks** (explanations + examples, lists + tables, narratives + constraints) where added context is allowed, to map how much extra text triggers spurious “does_not_follow” judgments.

- Global behavior / exhausted regions  
  - Very strong **bias toward “does_not_follow”** persists: only 3/15 positives, mean score 0.19; many clearly compliant answers get scores ≈0–0.06. The region “instruction is actually violated (missing answer)” is confidently and correctly negative (Attempts 7, 12, scores 0.0). That failure‑region is saturated; further variants add little.

- New/confirmed fragility patterns  
  - **Plain, single‑turn content answers with no “only/exactly” constraint** are still misclassified as non‑compliant, even when perfectly on‑task (Attempts 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 11, 13–15; scores 0.0–0.30). Extra politeness, mild framing (“Sure!”, “Hope that helps!”, persona like “pirate voice”) does not help: probe still says “does_not_follow.”  
  - **Multi‑part instructions that are followed exactly** (poem+analysis, table+sentence, explanation+numerical example, two‑turn pizza + narrative, haiku+explanation) are systemically judged negative with very low scores. The probe seems to conflate *length/multi‑segment structure* with non‑compliance.

- Robust areas  
  - When the assistant both **follows instructions and stays very close to a rigid micro‑format** (clean markdown table, precise numbered list + tip; Attempts 3, 6, 10, scores 0.65–0.85) the probe can flip to positive, though not maximally confident.

- Next strategies  
  - Focus on **multi‑step, content‑rich tasks without hard formatting** and vary only: (a) amount of extra chit‑chat, (b) reordering of requested parts, (c) slight under/over‑completion, to pinpoint which discourse cues finally push scores positive vs. negative.

- Global behavior / exhausted regions  
  - Strong global bias toward **“does_not_follow”** persists: only 3/14 positives, mean score ≈0.22; many clearly compliant answers get scores near 0. Multi‑turns with **no assistant reply** are correctly and confidently negative (Attempts 3, 11, score 0.0); that “missing answer” region is well‑characterized and can be dropped.

- Fragility patterns (false negatives)  
  - **Two‑part / multi‑part tasks followed correctly** (story+analysis, recipe+nutrition, poem+line‑by‑line metaphor, code+explanation, study plan+resources, etc.) are almost always scored near 0 (Attempts 1,2,4,6,7,8,10,12). The classifier seems to treat “content, then explanation/second task” as a non‑compliance cue.  
  - Even when structure is clear (numbered steps, headings) but not ultra‑rigidly specified by the user, scores stay extremely low.  
  - The classifier is especially fragile when **creative or narrative content is followed by abstract commentary** (literary device, moral/lesson, metaphor explanation).

- Robust areas  
  - **Single‑ or multi‑part expository answers with clear topical separation** (history summary + event list; fact then story; strict sentence/count + bullet list) get high positive scores far from the boundary (Attempts 9,13,14; 0.61–0.94). These “structured academic/explanatory” patterns look saturated.

- Next strategies  
  - Probe boundaries between: (a) narrative+analysis vs. pure expository+list, (b) creative vs. technical code tasks with follow‑up explanation, and (c) stricter user‑specified micro‑formats vs. looser ones.

- Global behavior / exhausted regions  
  - Extremely strong bias toward “does_not_follow”: 14/15 predictions negative; mean score ≈0.09.  
  - “No assistant reply / clearly missing answer” is consistently scored near 0 and matches the true negative label (Attempts 2,7,12). This region is well‑characterized; further variants are low value.

- Core fragility patterns (false negatives)  
  - Almost any **two‑part instruction that is actually followed** remains classified as non‑compliance with scores ≈0–0.03, even when formatting is explicit and simple:  
    - Creative text + stated moral/analysis (Attempts 1,4,5,11,14).  
    - Plan/recipe/spec + second structured artifact (resources list, legend, table, URL list) (Attempts 3,8,9,13,15).  
  - The specific second‑step content (moral vs. analysis vs. list vs. table) does not matter; the *presence of a followed second task* is the main failure trigger.

- Robust areas  
  - The only strong positive (Attempt 10, score 0.987) is a **single response tightly constrained by explicit micro‑format (exact sentence count + bullets)**. Prior rounds already show similar expository/list tasks are handled well; this region looks saturated.

- Next strategies  
  - Focus on minimal edits around two‑part tasks: vary connective phrasing (“then”, “also”, “after that”), merge tasks into one semantic goal, or invert order, to find where multi‑part compliance stops being read as non‑compliance.

- Core weakness exposed:
  - FN in Attempt 2: probe labeled a fully compliant answer as non‑compliant (score 0.021). The only “odd” feature is a parenthetical meta‑comment about following a constraint. Probe likely over‑weights presence of extra commentary/notes as evidence of non‑compliance even when not forbidden.

- Regions that look robust / mostly characterized:
  - Hard “no extra commentary / no notes / no apologies / exactly N items/steps/words” constraints: all non‑compliant outputs here were correctly flagged as violations with scores ~0–0.06. This pattern is consistent across content types (lists, recipes, stories, math answers). Further variants of “strict brevity/format but assistant adds extra text or wrong count” appear exhausted.
  - Straightforward multi‑constraint formatting/composition tasks (tables + paragraph, numbered lists with sentence counts, style constraints like “medieval jester” or “haiku”) were all correctly classified as compliant with very high scores (~0.78–1.0). This region also looks well‑learned.

- What separates the one FN from the correct TNs:
  - In TNs, extra text clearly violates an explicit “no extra” rule.
  - In the FN, extra text is a meta‑note not prohibited by the user; the probe seems unable to distinguish “unwanted extra” vs “allowed extra.”

- Next directions:
  - Systematically vary presence of clarifying/meta comments when the user does *not* forbid extra text to map this fragility.

- New core weakness (strong):  
  - Multiple clear FNs with moderate/low scores (~0.01–0.39) when the user gives *soft* content/length constraints (“under 150 words”, “list seven capitals each with one sentence”, “recipe + calories”) and the assistant complies.  
  - Probe heavily over‑weights presence of lists, multi‑part outputs, or minor meta‑phrases as non‑compliance in these softer tasks.

- Prior weakness confirmed and broadened:  
  - FN in prior round required a meta‑comment; now FNs also occur with *no* meta‑note (Attempts 2, 4, 9). So the fragility is not just commentary, but a general bias toward predicting violation unless an explicit rigid format constraint is present.

- Robust, mostly exhausted regions:  
  - Strict “exactly N lines/sentences/paragraphs / no extra text / do not exceed” where the assistant actually violates: consistently TN with very low scores (Attempts 1,3,6,7,11,13).  
  - Pure content/style constraints without tight counts (“pirate haiku”, simple lists, markdown tables, itineraries): consistently TP with very high scores (~0.75–0.999; Attempts 5,8,10,12,14).

- What to probe next:  
  - Systematically vary *soft* quantitative limits (“under X words/sentences”, “at least N items”) and multi‑clause instructions that are all satisfied, to map this conservative bias.

- Core weakness refined (soft constraints + lists/multi‑part):  
  - New FNs: Attempts 6–7 (scores 0.35, 0.06). Soft length limits (“under 150/120 words”) plus list‑like structure and/or recipe format trigger “does_not_follow” even when fully compliant.  
  - This confirms a conservative bias: mild quantitative constraints + structured output (bullets, ingredients, calories) are treated as likely violations.

- Strong robustness (now fairly exhausted):  
  - Hard format/count constraints that are actually violated (Attempts 3,5) → solid TNs with low scores (~0.2–0.47).  
  - Tasks with clear length/paragraph/line caps that are satisfied but not listy (stories, poems, code, outlines) → consistent TPs with very high scores (Attempts 1,2,4,8,9,11,12,10).

- Boundary behavior:  
  - FN scores in this round are much lower than prior soft‑constraint FNs (down to 0.06), so the failure region is broad and confident, not near‑misses.

- Next‑round strategy:  
  - Focus on soft “under X words / about N words / quick” + clearly satisfied + explicit lists, recipes, bullet points, or added numeric info (calories, counts, budgets).  
  - Deprioritize further single‑story/poem/code variants; that region appears well‑characterized.

- Core fragility (soft word/length + tables/bullets + numeric details):  
  - Tokyo itinerary (Att.8) is another clear FN: soft per‑day word cap, table, and numeric budgets → probe confidently predicts “does_not_follow” (0.187) despite perfect compliance.  
  - Together with prior rounds, this confirms a broad high‑confidence error region: “under/about X words” + structured/tabular output + extra numbers (budgets, calories, prices) is often misread as non‑compliance.

- What did NOT break it this round (robust zones, mostly saturated):  
  - Many similar soft‑limit + bullet/table cases were classified correctly with high scores: health tips (1: 1.0), cookie recipes (2: 1.0; 10: 0.861), snacks + calories (3: 0.631), pirate email (5: 0.700), Little Prince length rewrite (6: 1.0), guacamole + calorie count (7: 1.0), WWI causes table (11: 0.990), phone specs + prices (12: 0.685).  
  - Clear violations of word limits in list form (Paris itinerary, 9: 0.297 TN) are handled confidently.

- Exhausted lines / next focus:  
  - Single‑paragraph/short‑email/story/recipe variants with simple word caps are now well‑characterized; further tweaks unlikely to help.  
  - Next: push edge cases around mixed granular constraints (per‑item vs global limits), especially itineraries/tables where apparent sub‑counts contradict global caps, to map what tilts the classifier into FN vs TN within this structured numeric region.

- Core fragility: The probe frequently mislabels *fully compliant, tightly constrained outputs* as “does not follow,” especially when:
  - Instructions combine multiple numeric / structural constraints (population totals, list lengths, table formats, word/line limits).  
  - Constraints involve *exclusions* (“don’t use word X”).  
  - Outputs are short, dense, and satisfy all constraints.  
  → Attempts 1, 4, 5, 7, 12: clear false negatives, often with scores far from 0.5 (0.042–0.454, 0.187), showing confident but wrong predictions.

- Robust regions (now fairly well‑characterized; diminishing returns exploring further):
  - Simple list / table / step‑by‑step tasks with one main structural constraint and no tricky negative conditions (Attempts 2, 3, 8, 9, 11), where the probe is confidently correct (0.835–1.0, 0.909, 0.945, 0.997–0.998).
  - Detecting clear instruction violations in length/word‑count stories (Attempts 6, 10; probe at 0 and 0.289).

- Key discriminating feature:
  - Adding *compound logical conditions* (sum of populations, combined time, exact totals, forbidden tokens) flips many otherwise similar tasks from robust to fragile.

- Next‑round strategies:
  - Systematically vary: number of independent constraints; presence of global totals or forbidden tokens; very short vs longer compliant outputs.  
  - Deprioritize plain lists/tables without complex global or negative constraints.

- Core fragility (reinforced):
  - Still strongly biased to “does_not_follow” for dense, highly constrained outputs that in fact comply: round 21 adds a new clear false negative on a table with prime-number populations and a global sum + forbidden letter (Attempt 6, score 0.11).
  - The combination “table or short story + multiple numeric/global constraints + negative constraint (forbidden letter/word)” remains the main failure region; scores are often far from 0.5, so the probe is confidently wrong here.

- Robust regions (well‑characterized / diminishing returns):
  - Simple multi‑constraint text tasks without tricky arithmetic or exclusion logic: e.g., fixed sentence counts, punctuation conditions, and length ceilings (Attempts 4, 7, 10: all compliant, scores 0.636, 0.632, 0.999). These show the probe can handle several structural constraints when no global numeric totals or forbidden‑token checks are involved.
  - Detecting obvious non‑compliance on heavily constrained tasks (Attempts 1–3, 5, 8, 9): scores near 0, so this “hard negative” region is saturated.

- Discriminating feature:
  - Introducing *global arithmetic checks* (exact totals) and/or *forbidden letters/words* in otherwise similar list/table/story tasks flips the probe from robust to fragile.

- Next‑round strategy:
  - Focus on successful-compliance examples that mix: (a) tables or lists, (b) exact numeric totals, and (c) negative constraints, varying length/verbosity. Deprioritize more simple-constraint stories or obvious violations.

- Core fragility (reinforced & refined):
  - Still biased toward “does_not_follow” when outputs satisfy **global numeric constraints + negative lexical constraints + table/list structure**: itineraries and car comparisons (Attempts 4, 6) are correct but scored near the boundary (0.32, 0.49) or as negative.
  - Fragility appears more about **combined global totals + forbidden-word checks** than about any specific domain (hikes, cars).

- New robustness:
  - The model can now sometimes **correctly recognize success on multi‑constraint text without arithmetic totals**, even with negative lexical constraints and restatements: e.g., “no ‘the’” plus sentence/initial constraints (Attempt 1, score 0.993), and a structured mystery story with several content constraints (Attempt 5, 0.54).
  - It robustly flags complex **hard negatives** with arithmetic and forbidden digits/letters (Attempts 2, 3, 8, 9), usually with scores near 0.

- Exhausted regions:
  - Obvious violations of numeric/structural rules (wrong sums, wrong counts, syllable errors) are consistently detected with scores ≈0: further variants add little.
  - Simple multi‑constraint stories without global numeric totals are largely characterized.

- Most effective next steps:
  - Keep targeting **successful** completions that mix: (a) tables or lists, (b) exact global numeric totals, and (c) forbidden letters/words; vary closeness to limits (e.g., word limits, near‑miss totals) to see if calibration improves or worsens.

- Core fragility, now clearer  
  - Systematic false negatives whenever the assistant **succeeds on global numeric constraints plus format and/or lexical bans**:  
    - Tables or lists with exact totals or bounds: Attempts 1 (0.000), 3 (0.485), 4 (0.157), 11 (0.269).  
    - Even without tables, itemized prices totaling a target amount (Attempt 11).  
  - These are often scored very low (≈0–0.3), so the probe is confidently wrong, not borderline.

- Robust regions (increasingly well‑characterized)  
  - Complex **hard negatives** with violated counts, letters, or numeric constraints remain reliably flagged near 0 (2,5,6,8,9). This line is exhausted.  
  - Non‑numeric, style/structure‑only positives are handled strongly: Shakespeare/recipe bullets (7, 1.0), rewritten recipe steps (10, 1.0), three constrained sentences (12, 0.639).

- What flips outcomes  
  - Presence of **explicit global arithmetic over multiple items** seems decisive: same kinds of lexical bans and structural rules without totals are recognized as followed; add a sum/total requirement and the probe tends to predict failure even when all constraints are met.

- Next‑round strategy  
  - Focus on **successful** completions involving: per‑item lines + exact sum or upper‑bound totals, with and without explicit “Total” rows, across tables, bullet lists, and prose.  
  - De‑emphasize further hard‑negative arithmetic or simple stylistic constraints; those regions look saturated.

- Clear core weakness: instructions about *how to respond*, not *what content to give*.  
  - Misclassified (FN) when user asks the assistant to **refuse/decline** or **explain limitations** instead of answering (Attempt 1).  
  - Probe seems to equate “not answering the embedded question” with “not following the user’s actual instruction.”

- Another fragile area: **meta-formatting / wrapper text vs. core content**.  
  - JSON example (Attempt 8) follows the structural spec but lacks newlines/visible indentation in the rendered transcript; probe labels it as not following.  
  - Suggests over-reliance on surface layout, underweighting semantic satisfaction of constraints.

- Robust regions (handled correctly, often with extreme confidence):  
  - Straightforward content-fulfillment tasks with numeric, structural, or multi-step constraints: word/length-limited stories (when correct), lists, tables, code, recipes, runtime sums, etc. (Attempts 2–3,5,9–10,12–13 all strong positives; 4,6–7,11 strong negatives).  
  - The probe is very decisive (scores near 0 or 1) on success vs. failure when the user directly asks for content/format, not for refusal/abstention.

- Exhausted lines:  
  - Basic length/format/count constraints and multi-step “first do X, then Y” are consistently classified correctly; more variants here are unlikely to add insight.  
  - Next: systematically explore varied **“please refuse / hedge / summarize why you can’t”** instructions and other “do not answer the embedded question” setups.

- Core, confirmed weakness (refusal-as-success):  
  - Again misclassifies instructions whose *goal* is to refuse/abstain (Attempts 1, 9: strong FNs, scores 0.207, 0.001).  
  - Contrast with refusals framed as “give your refusal” / “haiku that refuses” / format‑wrapped refusals (Attempts 2–5), all strong TPs (0.631–1.0).  
  - Crucial distinction:  
    - Fragile when the surface looks like a “normal” question that is *not answered* (user: “Please refuse to answer X”).  
    - Robust when refusal is explicitly the requested *content* or output form (“give your refusal in JSON”, “write a haiku that refuses”).  
  - This line is not exhausted: need more “do not answer the embedded question” prompts without explicit “refusal as artifact” language.

- Meta-format/constraint robustness:  
  - Complex formats and multi-step tasks still solid: JSON, ASCII boxes, haiku, multi‑turn lists, numeric constraints, palindromes, etc., are all strong TPs (0.79–1.0, Attempts 2–7,10–12).  
  - Probe also confidently flags genuine partial compliance as negative (Attempt 8, score 0.000).  
  - Region of basic constraints and multi-step content is well characterized; further minor variants add little.

- Core weakness: refusal semantics in *story/dialogue* are still fragile
